II. PRELIMINARIES

In this section, we introduce the problem setting (Section II-A) and we provide required background on SOS optimization (Section II-B).

A. Problem setting

Throughout most of the paper, we consider continuous-time systems with rational system dynamics of the form

$$\dot{x} = f_r(x) + g_r(x) u$$

$$= 
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{a_1(x)}{d_1(x)} & \cdots & \frac{b_{11}(x)}{e_{11}(x)} & \cdots & \frac{b_{1m}(x)}{e_{1m}(x)} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\frac{a_n(x)}{d_n(x)} & \cdots & \frac{b_{n1}(x)}{e_{n1}(x)} & \cdots & \frac{b_{nm}(x)}{e_{nm}(x)}
\end{bmatrix}
u$$ (1)

with the state vector $x(t) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, its derivative $\dot{x}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and the control input $u(t) \in \mathbb{R}^m$, all at time $t \geq 0$, where we omit the time index to keep the notation simple. Further, $d_i(x)$, $b_{ij}(x)$, $e_{ij}(x)$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$ and $j = 1, \ldots, m$, are polynomials with degree greater than or equal to zero, and $a_i(x)$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, are polynomials with degree greater than zero. The latter is necessary because, for simplicity, we assume the origin to be a steady-state. Any $\dot{x}$, $x$, $u$ satisfying (1) also fulfill the polynomial equation

$$p(x) \dot{x} =
\begin{bmatrix}
a_1(x) p_1(x) \\
\vdots \\
a_n(x) p_n(x)
\end{bmatrix}$$

$$+ 
\begin{bmatrix}
b_{11}(x) p_{11}(x) & \cdots & b_{1m}(x)p_{1m}(x) \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
b_{n1}(x) p_{n1}(x) & \cdots & b_{nm}(x)p_{nm}(x)
\end{bmatrix}
u$$ (2)

with

$$p(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n d_i(x) \prod_{j=1}^m e_{ij}(x),$$

$$p_i(x) = \frac{p(x)}{d_i(x)},$$

$$p_{ij}(x) = \frac{p(x)}{e_{ij}(x)}$$

We assume $p(x) \neq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ which is equivalent to assuming $d_i(x), e_{ij}(x) \neq 0$ for all $i, j$, and thus, implies that the vector field in (1) is globally defined. Then, we define

$$[ \mathcal{P} \quad 1 ] 
\begin{bmatrix}
z_p(x) \\
1
\end{bmatrix}
=
p(x), $$

$$\mathcal{B}H(x) =
\begin{bmatrix}
b_{11}(x) p_{11}(x) & \cdots & b_{1m}(x)p_{1m}(x) \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
b_{n1}(x) p_{n1}(x) & \cdots & b_{nm}(x)p_{nm}(x)
\end{bmatrix},$$

where $\mathcal{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times N_z}$, $\mathcal{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times N_u}$ and $\mathcal{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times N_p}$ are unknown parameters representing the coefficients of the polynomials in (2), $Z(x)$ is an $N_z \times 1$ vector of monomials in $x$, $Z_p(x)$ is an $N_p \times 1$ vector of monomials in $x$, and $H(x)$ is an $N_u \times m$ matrix of monomials in $x$. For instance, in case that the system dynamics (1) are of a scalar and second-order polynomial form, then we have $Z(x) = H(x) = \begin{bmatrix} x & x^2 \end{bmatrix}^T$ and $Z_p(x) = 0$. Throughout this paper, we assume that $Z(x)$, $Z_p(x)$, and $H(x)$ are known, although our arguments remain valid if they are over-approximated, i.e., if additional monomials are added which are not present in the actual unknown system dynamics. This translates into assuming that the basis functions of the numerators and denominators in (1) are known or over-approximated. Moreover, $Z(x)$ and $Z_p(x)$ only contain monomials with a minimum degree of one such that $Z(x)$ is zero if and only if $x=0$ and we can decompose $Z(x)$ as $Z(x) = Y(x)x$ for a matrix $Y(x)$ of dimension $N_z \times n$, and similarly for $Z_p(x)$.

Using these definitions, we can rewrite (2) as

$$[ \mathcal{P} \quad 1 ] 
\begin{bmatrix}
z_p(x) \\
1
\end{bmatrix}
\dot{x} = A Z(x) + B H(x) u$$

(3)

where $\mathcal{P}$, $\mathcal{A}$, and $\mathcal{B}$ are unknown parameters and $Z_p(x)$, $Z(x)$, and $H(x)$ are known polynomial basis matrices. This representation is advantageous over (1) because it is linearly parametrized in the unknown variables. In this paper, we present an approach for designing polynomial state-feedback controllers $u(x) = K(x)Z(x)$ for the considered rational system (1) with robust stability guarantees, using no model knowledge but only one open-loop data trajectory. However, instead of assuming that the data are generated exactly by the rational system dynamics (1), i.e., they satisfy (3), we allow for a perturbation of (3) taking the form

$$[ \mathcal{P} \quad 1 ] 
\begin{bmatrix}
z_p(x) \\
1
\end{bmatrix}
\dot{x} = A Z(x) + B H(x) u + B_w w$$

(4)

where $w(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{m_w}$, $t \geq 0$, describes an unknown disturbance sequence perturbing the polynomial equation (3). We assume that the matrix $B_w$ is known and has full column rank. If $B_w$ does not satisfy the rank assumption, the disturbance can be transformed into $\tilde{w} = B_w w$ with $\tilde{B}_w = I$ and a quadratic noise bound on the sequence of $\tilde{w}$. In this paper, we use a finite input-state-trajectory $\{x(t_k), \dot{x}(t_k), u(t_k)\}_{k=1}^N$ with sampling times $\{t_k\}_{k=1}^N$ satisfying (4) for some unknown disturbance $\{\tilde{w}(t_k)\}_{k=1}^N$ which satisfies a known quadratic bound defined via the matrix $\tilde{W} = \begin{bmatrix} \tilde{w}(t_1) & \tilde{w}(t_2) & \cdots & \tilde{w}(t_N) \end{bmatrix}$.

Using that \(p(x)^{2}\neq0\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), this implies stability for any \(\begin{bmatrix}A&B&P\end{bmatrix}\in\Sigma_{A,B,P}\). Asymptotic stability follows for \(\varepsilon>0\), which thus concludes the proof.

Note that the polynomial matrix \(Q(x)\) in (7) is not linear in the decision variables \(\mathcal{V}\) and \(K(x)\) and hence, for a practical implementation, it needs to be transformed into a linear SOS condition. This is possible following standard steps from model-based robust control of linear systems (compare [20]): Defining the new variable \(L(x)=K(x)Y_{K}(x)\mathcal{V}, Q(x)\) is linear in the decision variables \(\mathcal{V}, L(x)\), and \(\tau\). After finding variables \(\mathcal{V}, L(x)\), and \(\tau\) such that \(Q(x)\) is SOS, a controller stabilizing the unknown system can be implemented as

\[
u(x) = K(x)Z_{K}(x) = K(x)Y_{K}(x)x = L(x)\mathcal{V}^{-1}x. \]
(9)

Hence, Theorem 5 provides a simple and direct method to design a controller which robustly stabilizes the rational System (1) for all matrices which are consistent with the data and the noise bound. Moreover, the number of decision variables of the proposed SOS program is independent of the data length which allows us to consider large data sets for the controller design. More precisely, the feasibility problem in Theorem 5 has overall \(1 + \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + mN_{K}\) decision variables, i.e., the number of decision variables scales quadratically with the system order \(n\) as in standard robust control and linearly with the number of monomials in \(Z_{K}(x)\).

Theorem 5 reduces to a recently obtained result in [15] for polynomial system dynamics, i.e., if \(d_{i}(x)=e_{ij}(x)=1\) for all \(i=1,\ldots,n\) and \(j=1,\ldots,m\). The above result is not a straightforward consequence of the result in [15] due to the role of the polynomial \(p(x)\) in the proof. More precisely, only by combining the bound on \([A\quad B\quad P]\) in Theorem 4 with the fact that a quadratic Lyapunov function is used, we can obtain (8) via the identity

\[
(I_{n}\otimes P)(I_{n}\otimes Z_{p}(x)) + I_{n} = p(x)I_{n}
\]

in the proof. If, e.g., more general polynomial Lyapunov functions \(V(x)=Z(x)^{T}X(x)Z(x)\) are used, the partial derivatives \(\frac{\partial{Z(x)}}{\partial{x}}\) prohibit this argument and thus, an extension of our results to polynomial Lyapunov functions is an interesting issue for future research.

An additional advantage of our approach is that the above arguments follow the line of LMI-based robust control techniques from [20] and it is straightforward to extend them to more general problem formulations such as including prior knowledge on the system (cf. [6]) or designing a controller which not only stabilizes the closed loop but also enforces a desired performance specification. To this end, we consider robust quadratic performance (cf. [20]) with index \(\begin{bmatrix}Q_{p} & S_{p}\\ S_{p}^{\top} & R_{p}\end{bmatrix}, R_{p} \succ 0\), for the system \(\dot{x}=f_{r}(x)+g_{r}(x)u+\matrix Q_{p}\ 0 & S_{p}\\ * & S_{p}^{\top} -B^{-\intercal} 0 & *\\ * & * &-Q_{p} \\ * & * &* - p\left(\frac{q(x)}{p^{2}}\right)\)

For instance, \(Q_{p}=-\gamma^{2}I\), \(S_{p}=0\), \(R_{p}=I\) corresponds to an \(\mathcal{L}_{2}\)-gain bound \(\gamma\) on \(w_{p}\mapsto z_{p}\). Following similar arguments as in Theorem 5, it can be shown that robust quadratic performance holds for the channel \(w_{p}\mapsto z_{p}\) if there exist variables \(\mathcal{V}, L(x)\) and \(\tau\) such that

\[\begin{bmatrix}Q(x) & * & *& *\\ -B^{\prime\prime} \star & S_{p}q_{3}(x) \star & B^{\prime\prime}q_{2}(x)^{\prime} \star & B^{\prime\prime}q_{1}(x)^{I} \star \\ q_{3}(x) & q_{3}(x)q_{2}(x)^{\prime \intercal}  I & -Q_{p} & *\\ -B^{\prime\prime} \star & p_{3}(x)q_{1}(x)^{\prime \intercal} \star\\ S_{p} & B^{\prime\prime} q_{3}^{\intercal} & D_{p}\xrightarrow{S Q} & T_{p}\xrightarrow{G}I \end{bmatrix}.\]
(10)

is SOS, where \(q_{3}(x)=CY(x)\mathcal{V}+DL(x)\) and \(Q_{p}=Q_{p}+S_{p}D_{p}+D_{p}^{\intercal}S_{p}^{\intercal}\). If this problem is feasible, then the controller in (9) guarantees quadratic performance robustly for all rational systems which are consistent with the measured data and the noise level. The proof of this fact is omitted due to space reasons.

We note that the authors in [13] use related tools to analyze discrete-time polynomial systems w.r.t. dissipativity properties but an extension to controller design in discrete-time is challenging.

C. Numerical example

Finally, we illustrate the applicability of the proposed approach with two numerical examples: an academic example as well as a realistic model used for drug distribution [24]. For the latter, we also incorporate performance specifications. The simulations in this paper are implemented in MATLAB using YALMIP [25] with its SOS module [26] and the solver MOSEK [27].

Example 6. Consider the rational system

\[\dot{x}_{1} = \frac{x_{2}^{2}}{1 + x_{1}^{2}} + u_{1}, \]

\[\dot{x}_{2} = x_{1}x_{2} + x_{2}u_{2}.\]

according to (2), any trajectory of this system also satisfies

\[(1 + x_{1}^{2})\dot{x}_{1} = x_{2}^{2} + (1 + x_{1}^{2})u_{1}, \]

\[ (1 + x_{1}^{2})\dot{x}_{2} = x_{1}x_{2} + x_{1}^{3}x_{2} + (x_{2} + x_{1}^{2}x_{2})u_{2}.\]

Following Section II-A, we define the true (unknown) system matrices \(A = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\), and \(P = 1\), and the vectors of monomials \(Z(x) = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} & x_{2} & x_{2}^{2} & x_{1}x_{2}\\ 1 & x_{1}^{2} & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & x_{2} & 0\end{bmatrix}^{\intercal}\). Note that this system violates our standing assumption \(p(x) \neq 0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\) . Nevertheless, as we show in the following, the presented approach can be used to successfully design a robust controller with local closed-loop stability and good practical performance. For the data generation, we proceed as for Example 6 with \(\bar{w} = 1 \times 10^{- 1}\) and \(d = 40\) trajectories of length \(N_{d} = 5\) sampled uniformly from \(x(t_{0}) \in [- 2, 2]^{2}\) , \(u(t_{k}) \in [- 5, 5]\) and \(\| \hat{w} (t_{k})\|_{2} \leq \bar{w}\) for \(k = 1, \ldots , N_{d}\)  

We choose \(Q_{p} = - \gamma^{2} I\) , \(S_{p} = 0\) , \(R_{p} = I\) , \(B_{p} = I\) , and \(z_{p} = x\) such that our design objective is an \(\mathcal{L}_{2}\) - gain bound of \(\gamma = 400\) on the channel \(w_{p} \mapsto x\) . Then, we solve (10) to obtain a controller. The phase portrait of the resulting closed-loop behavior with the controller designed using (10) is depicted in Fig. 1. It shows that the controller stabilizes the system at the origin for \(x \in (- 5, 5) \times (- 5, 15)\) even though \(p(x) \neq 0\) is not satisfied globally. To illustrate the benefits of the performance criterion, we also compute a stabilizing controller based on (7). Compared to this controller, the controller computed via (10) leads to a 20% reduction of the \(\mathcal{L}_{2}\) - norm of the performance output \(z_{p}\) . For this example, (10) is solvable in less than one second.  

## IV. BEYOND POLYNOMIAL BASIS FUNCTIONS  

In this section, we propose a data-driven control approach for systems which are linear in general, possibly nonpolynomial basis functions. The main idea relies on lifting the nonlinear system to an extended state-space with polynomial dynamics and then applying the results of Section III for robust controller design.  

In the following, we consider nonlinear systems  

\[\dot{\xi} = f(\xi) + g(\xi)u, \quad (13)\]
